problems.description: Default DATABASE renamed todos.db -> tasks.db silently changes the on-disk data path for any existing deployment.
test_app.py sets os.environ['DATABASE'] = '' at module level before importing app — a fragile side-effectful import pattern, and the empty-string value is confusing (any non-'todos.db' would do).

Convention score 0.70 with 9 violations, but 7 are in untouched files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py); the app.py/test_app.py violations flagged are not introduced by this diff (no classes are added here).

strengths: Fixes a real bug: newly created tasks defaulted to status 'done' instead of 'pending'
Adds a comprehensive 14-test suite covering happy paths and error cases (400/404, missing/empty/whitespace titles)
Small, focused diff (+142/-2 across 2 files) with no new dependencies
Tests follow existing Flask patterns: app_context fixture, tempfile-backed DB, pytest conventions
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-scoped commit that fixes a status default bug and adds solid test coverage; the 0.70 convention score largely reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files, so the commit's own code is effectively cleaner than that measurement suggests.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET_KEY falls back to a hardcoded 'dev-secret-change-me-...' value; if deployed without the env var set, tokens are forgeable. Acceptable for a seed app but worth flagging.

current_user_id() returns None for an unknown identity, which flows into get_tasks(None)/SQL param and yields an empty result instead of a 401; a type guard (int | None) is returned but routes assume an int.

Discrepancy: convention score 0.70 is driven almost entirely by pre-existing violations in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, test_app.py); the only app.py flag ('Classes should use PascalCase') matches no class introduced here — the diff itself is consistently snake_case.

No test coverage added for the new auth flows (register/login/ownership scoping) despite the codebase shipping tests; this is the story session's job, but leaving it for a later session increases regression risk.

strengths: Multi-user data isolation via owner_id scoping on every task query/update — a real security improvement over the single-tenant baseline.
Backward-compatible schema migration (PRAGMA table_info check + ALTER TABLE) preserves pre-existing rows and repeated-init safety.
Passwords hashed with werkzeug generate_password_hash rather than stored in plaintext.
Follows existing single-file patterns faithfully: get_db() context manager, dict(row) row handling, parameterized SQL, snake_case helpers.
Clean auth surface with explicit 400/401/409 error paths and JWT expiry/invalid-token callbacks.
commit_reviews.summary: A faithful, well-scoped feature addition — JWT auth plus per-user ownership — that respects the seed's single-file patterns and keeps data isolated; the low convention score is largely pre-existing debt in untouched files, not introduced by this commit.

problems.description: The 0.70 convention score is inflated by false positives: celery_config.py's 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE' flags broker_url/result_backend/etc., but Celery's config_from_object requires lowercase attribute names, so these are not real violations.
Most 'Classes should use PascalCase' flags (app.py, test_app.py) and the repositories.py constant flag are pre-existing or spurious — this diff adds no classes and does not touch repositories.py.

Silent email fabrication fallback f'{username}@example.com' in create_user and _trigger_completion_notification would route notifications to a bogus address in a real deployment; acceptable only because the email send is mocked.
Broker and result backend are hardcoded to redis://localhost:6379/0 in celery_config.py with no environment override, coupling the app to a fixed local Redis.
edit_task now issues an extra SELECT (get_task) before every update purely to guard the notification transition; minor but avoidable overhead on the hot path.

strengths: Clean async decoupling — Celery moves the email side-effect off the request path with a clear module split (celery_config.py vs celery_tasks.py).
Completion-transition guard (before/after status comparison) correctly prevents duplicate notifications on repeated completes.
Hermetic, broker-free tests: task_always_eager + monkeypatched .delay assert the notification contract without a running Redis/Celery.
DB migration mirrors the existing _tasks_has_owner_id pattern and preserves existing rows via ALTER TABLE, respecting established conventions.
Uses existing infrastructure idioms throughout: get_db(), jwt_required(), current_user_id(), and the established test fixture setup.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured feature commit that fits the notification-service story with clean layering, a guarded trigger, and hermetic tests — the 0.70 convention score is a measurement artifact since the flagged constants are mandatory Celery config keys and several violations hit pre-existing files.

problems.description: BaseRepository ABC with an abstract table_name property is speculative generality — an abstract base over just two small concrete repositories adds indirection and a forced inheritance contract without demonstrated payoff for a single-file Flask app.
The new repositories.py introduces a module-level constant that violates UPPER_CASE naming (per convention measurement), contributing to the 0.70 convention score.
SonarQube delta shows +3 new smells introduced by this commit despite +0 bugs and no complexity change.
The refactor relocates all SQL/data-access logic into repositories.py without adding unit tests for the new layer; it relies on existing route-level coverage in test_app.py.

Discrepancy: the measured 0.70 convention score and 9 violations include files this commit did not touch (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, test_app.py); the commit's own footprint is limited to repositories.py and app.py.

strengths: Removes dead code: the _legacy_format_date helper, the unused _notify_admin stub, and unused imports (datetime, generate_password_hash).
Centralizes all SQL behind repository classes so route handlers no longer touch SQLite directly — a genuine separation-of-concerns improvement matching the updated docstring.
Keeps the route handlers and get_db() accessor intact, making this an incremental, low-risk refactor.
Docstring updated in the same commit to accurately describe the new repositories/routes/error-handling structure.
commit_reviews.summary: A sound layering refactor that moves SQL out of the route layer and removes dead code, but it introduces a speculative ABC abstraction and adds convention violations and +3 smells in the new module.

problems.description: The /tasks GET response shape changed from a bare list to an envelope object ({"data", "next_cursor", "total"}) with no versioning or compatibility shim. In a multi-session story, earlier sessions' consumers (frontend or integration tests) expecting the old list shape will break silently; only in-session tests were updated.

RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URL defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0 — the same shared finops-redis instance the story test harness flushes (flushdb/flushall, per repo operational notes). Concurrent sessions can wipe the rate-limit store mid-test causing flaky 429s, and flask-limiter fails closed if Redis is absent. The app's only storage dependency was previously SQLite.

rate_limit_key swallows all decode_token exceptions via `except Exception: pass`. Behavior (fall back to IP key) is fine, but narrowing to the documented JWT exceptions would avoid masking unrelated errors on every request path.

Measured convention score is 0.70 with 9 violations, but the flagged files (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE) are pre-existing and untouched by this diff. The commit's own additions (RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URL, RATE_LIMIT_DEFAULT, snake_case functions, zero new classes) conform — the low score overstates this commit's contribution.

strengths: Keyset pagination (id < cursor, ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT limit+1) avoids OFFSET scaling problems and the no-overlap page test guards against duplicates.
Rate limiting keys per authenticated user and falls back to IP, with env-configurable limits/storage, headers_enabled, and a 429 handler consistent with the existing _invalid_token_callback pattern.
list_by_owner_paginated follows the existing TaskRepository/_connect() pattern; limit is clamped to 1-100 and invalid cursor returns 400.
Tests are thorough: cursor walking, limit clamping, empty-list envelope, no-overlap, and memory:// storage override plus limiter.reset() keep tests hermetic.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-scoped session 5 that cleanly fits the route→repository architecture and follows existing conventions with solid tests, held back only by an unversioned breaking change to the /tasks response contract and a rate-limiter defaulting to the shared 6379 Redis store.

compounding_issues: Hardcoded dev JWT_SECRET_KEY fallback introduced in S2 was never hardened in S3-S5, leaving forgeable tokens if deployed without env vars
Email fabrication fallback (f'{username}@example.com') from S2/S3 persisted through S5, silently routing notifications to fake addresses
redis://localhost:6379/0 defaults appeared in S3 (celery) and S5 (rate limiter) — the shared finops-redis instance the story harness flushes, a latent infrastructure coupling
S5 changed GET /tasks from a bare list to an envelope (data/next_cursor/total) with no versioning or backward-compat path, breaking the contract earlier sessions built on
S4's BaseRepository ABC with abstract table_name is speculative generality over just two small repos; convention score sagged to 0.6 and +3 Sonar smells with no functional gain
key_decisions: S1 fixed the seed's 'done' default-status bug and built a 14-test suite up front, establishing testing as the spine (grew to 38 passing tests by S5)
S2 introduced per-user ownership (users table + tasks.owner_id) with an idempotent PRAGMA/ALTER-TABLE in-place migration, a pattern reused cleanly in S3 for the email column
S2 chose JWT auth via flask_jwt_extended and kept a single-file model layer, deferring structure to a later dedicated refactor session
S3 decoupled notifications with Celery .delay() on task-completion, wiring async email without blocking the request path
S4 extracted a Repository pattern (TaskRepository/UserRepository) into repositories.py, moving all SQL out of the route layer and enabling S5's pagination in the repository
S5 keyed the rate limiter on decoded JWT identity per-user and implemented cursor-based pagination with keyset id < cursor ordering
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality steadily improved across the five sessions. Tests climbed monotonically (13→23→27→27→38) and code grew from 146 to 466 lines with all sessions succeeding and a 0.96 cache hit rate for a total cost of just $0.13. S1-S3 layered features cleanly (greenfield bug fix, JWT auth, async email integration), each commit narrowly scoped with no regressions; the arc shows a mild dip in S4 where the refactor added three Sonar smells and a speculative abstract base without functional benefit, but S5 recovered with the strongest architecture fit (0.85), the largest test expansion, and a properly layered three-file structure. The persistent weaknesses are the unhardened dev JWT secret, the fabricated-email fallback, and — most notably — S5's unversioned API response-shape change, which introduces a compatibility break at the very end of an otherwise disciplined build-up.
story_review.summary: A coherent, low-cost, well-tested incremental build (greenfield → auth → async integration → refactor → cross-cutting) that steadily improved quality, with the main blemishes being a late unversioned API contract change and unresolved dev-secret/Redis-coupling debt carried from earlier sessions.
